About us

Waitaha Canterbury region is like no other, and we are proud to call it home. We work with Papatipu Rūnanga, stakeholders and the wider community to shape a thriving and resilient region, now and for future generations. Toitū te marae o Tāne, toitū te marae o Tangaroa, toitū te iwi. As a regional council, we’ve organised our work around the core services we provide - what we’re fundamentally here to do, and why. We’re focused on the social, economic, environmental and cultural impact our work will contribute to the community and the region. We’ve grouped our responsibilities into three areas: Environmental Regulation and Protection Ngā mahi tiakina me ngā whakaritenga taiao We are an environmental regulator, responsible for managing natural resources including air, soil, water and land. We work with mana whenua, stakeholders and communities to promote the sustainable management of these natural resources, and protect and enhance the health of our natural environment. Community Preparedness and Response to Hazards Te whakarite hapori me ngā urupare mōrearea We support the community to be prepared for and able to respond to natural and human-induced hazards and events. Our focus in flood and river resilience is advocating to Central Government for co-investment opportunities, planning and preparedness, and delivering on required outcomes. Public Transport Ngā waka tūmatanui As New Zealand’s largest region and home to its second-largest city, Waitaha/Canterbury needs robust public transport services to support growth and keep communities connected. We want more people to use public transport more often so they can access key centres and opportunities, quickly and conveniently.

    560+ runners turned our regional park into a finish line ⬇️ On Sunday, we hosted our inaugural McLeans Forest Run, held in the heart of McLeans Island Park. With 560+ runners in attendance, the event gave the running community a chance to experience the diverse forest landscape we manage and care for every day. It's easy to think of a regional park as just green space. But events like this show that they are much more. Regional parks are one of the few "third places" left, somewhere outside home and work where community forms naturally, surrounded by the unique biodiversity Canterbury has to offer. Thank you to everyone who ran, volunteered, and showed up. Catch you at the next one!💚

    Fencing… without the fence? We've partnered with Gallagher on a virtual fencing trial in Banks Peninsula to protect springhead wetlands. On Ian Lloyd's farm, around 100 cattle now wear GPS collars. Here's how it works: ➡️ Grazing boundaries are set from a phone app ➡️ Stock are guided by sound and a mild pulse if they push past. Virtual fencing lets farmers keep stock out of sensitive areas that were once too costly and labour-intensive to fence. Technology like this could change how we protect places like the Peninsula's wetlands. It's a glimpse of where farming's headed, and a chance to help shape it. eShepherd Virtual Fencing

    How did wallabies spread so far? It comes down to a single turning point: When coordinated management was removed. Wallabies escaped control and spread across thousands of hectares of ideal habitat. Once a population establishes, eradication becomes far harder and far more costly. But now that story is changing. A new, collaborative approach leads the way. By working together across farms, communities, and agencies, we're building a moving line of defence that pushes wallabies back. Proving that coordinated action delivers results where fragmented effort fails. Spotted a wallaby? Report it. Every sighting helps hold the line.

    Reaching zero wallabies takes all of us. Real progress happens when landowners, communities, and control teams work as one. By raising awareness and acting fast, we're protecting native ecosystems and farmland from one of the region's most damaging invasive pests, and the results speak for themselves: ➡️ Healthier farms ➡️ Better pasture ➡️ Fewer pests It's proof that small actions, like spotting and reporting a sighting, make a big difference. Spotted a wallaby? Report it. Every sighting brings us closer to zero.

    One team. One goal: zero wallabies. Behind every successful eradication effort is a coordinated team and the right technology. Through innovation and high-tech coordination, our crew is working to remove every last wallaby — protecting native ecosystems and farmland from one of the region's most damaging invasive pests. The tools driving success: ➡️ Thermal drones ➡️ Helicopters ➡️ Boots on the ground ➡️ Strengthened exclusion fencing This is what teamwork and innovation look like in practice, and it's powering the push to zero.
